title: Breakers, bulkheads, shedding and metastable failures
summary: Circuit breakers that fail fast, bulkheads that contain a slow dependency, admission control that sheds the least important work first, graceful degradation, and the retry storm that keeps a system down after its trigger is gone.

steps.title: The circuit breaker
body: When a dependency is failing, calling it anyway wastes your threads and adds load to something already
on its knees. A **circuit breaker** sits around the call and remembers recent results:
```text
failures pass the threshold
CLOSED  ───────────────────────────────>  OPEN      every call fails fast, no network
│ the probe succeeds                     │ the break time is over
│                                        v
└──────────────────────────────────  HALF-OPEN   let one probe (or a few) through
the probe fails: back to OPEN
Real breakers (Polly's, for example) trip on a **failure ratio** over a sampling window with a **minimum
throughput**, so two failures at 3 a.m. do not open it. While open, the caller uses a **fallback**: a cached
value, a default, or a clear error. The breaker protects the caller (no threads stuck waiting) and gives the
dependency room to recover. The **Integration** topic shows breakers in route code; here we care about
what they do to a whole system.

steps.prompt: A breaker with a threshold of 3 consecutive failures and a 10 s break. Put what happens in order.
lines: Three calls in a row time out while the breaker is closed
The breaker opens; for 10 s every call fails at once without touching the network
The break time ends and the breaker goes half-open
One probe call is let through and succeeds
The breaker closes and traffic flows normally again

steps.title: Bulkheads, shedding and back-pressure
body: - **Bulkhead**: separate pools (threads, connections, concurrency limits) per dependency, like the watertight
compartments of a ship. If recommendations hang, they use up *their* 20 slots, not the 200 that checkout needs.
- **Load shedding / admission control**: when you are at capacity, refuse new work **early and cheaply**
(429 or 503 in a millisecond) instead of queueing it until it times out. A request that waits longer than
the client will wait is pure waste: you do the work and nobody reads the answer.
- **Shed by priority**: drop best-effort work first (prefetch, analytics beacons), then normal, keep
critical (checkout, login) to the end.
- **Back-pressure**: let the slow end push back (bounded queues, `reject-publish`, 429 with `Retry-After`)
so producers slow down instead of buffers growing until something runs out of memory.
Adaptive concurrency limits (the idea behind TCP congestion control, applied to requests) lower the
number of in-flight requests when latency rises and raise it when things are healthy.

steps.prompt: Match each pattern to what it protects against.
pairs: Waiting on, and adding load to, a dependency that is already failing
One slow dependency using up the threads every other feature needs
Queueing work you cannot finish before the client gives up
Buffers growing without limit between a fast producer and a slow consumer
Retries multiplying the load during an outage

steps.title: Degrade gracefully
body: Decide, per feature, what happens when its dependency is gone. Most pages are made of parts that matter
very differently:
```text
product page                         dependency down → what the user sees
title, price, stock, Buy button    catalog, pricing → error page (cannot sell without them)
reviews                            reviews          → last cached copy, or hidden
"customers also bought"           recommendations  → a generic best-sellers list
delivery estimate                  shipping         → "usually 2-4 days"
**Serving stale** is often the best fallback: a cache that keeps expired entries and serves them while the
origin is down (`stale-if-error` on a CDN does exactly this). Write the fallback down in the design, and
test it, or it will not work on the day.

steps.prompt: Its dependency is down. Should the feature degrade or fail clearly?
items: The stock check before an order is accepted
steps.explain: Degrade where an older or generic answer is still useful. Fail clearly where a guess would be wrong: taking an order without stock or payment, or logging someone in without checking.

steps.title: Metastable failures: when the trigger is not the cause
body: Some outages keep going after their trigger is gone. Researchers named these **metastable failures**
(Bronson et al., HotOS 2021): a trigger pushes the system into a bad state, and a **sustaining effect** keeps
it there.
```text
14:00  a slow query makes the DB 4x slower                    the trigger
14:00  requests time out; clients retry 3x                    load x3
14:01  the slow query is killed: DB back to normal speed      trigger gone
14:01  load is still 3x capacity, so requests still time out, so clients still retry ...
14:40  someone sheds load at the gateway; the DB recovers in 30 s
Here the sustaining effect is **retries plus timeouts**: work done for requests the client already gave up
on is wasted, so goodput collapses while the DB is 100% busy. Other sustaining effects: a cold cache that
cannot warm because the DB is overloaded, and GC thrash from deep queues. The fix is to make load drop
below capacity: shed at the edge, open breakers, cap retries with budgets, bound queues. Adding capacity
works too, but usually takes longer than shedding.

prompt: **Symptom first.** From a postmortem timeline. Why did the outage last 37 more minutes after the trigger was
removed at 14:03?
code: 14:00:10  orders-db p99 rises from 8 ms to 900 ms (a migration locks a hot table)
14:00:40  api error rate 45%; api retries: 3 per request, no backoff
14:03:30  orders-db cpu 100%, active connections 800/800, error rate 52%
14:20:00  api pods scaled from 20 to 40; error rate 61%
14:40:00  gateway rate limit set to 60% of normal traffic
options: Retries kept the offered load above the database's capacity, so it stayed overloaded after the lock was gone; shedding load let it recover
The migration was not really cancelled until 14:40
40 API pods were still too few
The rate limit fixed a bug in the database
steps.explain: The trigger ended at 14:03, but every timed-out request became three, so the database never got below 100%. Doubling the API pods made it worse: more callers, more retries, more connections. Only cutting the offered load broke the loop. Action items: retry budgets with jitter, a breaker on the DB calls, admission control at the gateway.

steps.title: A circuit breaker
prompt: Write a class `CircuitBreaker` with an injected clock (times in ms are passed in):
- `CircuitBreaker(int failureThreshold, long breakMs)`, starting `"Closed"`;
- `string State`: `"Closed"`, `"Open"` or `"HalfOpen"`;
- `bool Allow(long nowMs)`: Closed → true. Open → if `breakMs` have passed since it opened, become HalfOpen
and return true (that is the one probe); otherwise false. HalfOpen → false (the probe is still out);
- `void Success()`: HalfOpen → Closed; in Closed it resets the failure count;
- `void Failure(long nowMs)`: HalfOpen → Open again from `nowMs`; Closed → count it, and on reaching
`failureThreshold` **consecutive** failures open from `nowMs`.
Production breakers use a failure ratio over a time window with a minimum throughput; consecutive
failures keep this one small.
solution: public string State { get; private set; } = "Closed";
if (State == "Open" && nowMs - openedAt >= breakMs) { State = "HalfOpen"; return true; }
hints: Keep the state, a consecutive-failure counter and the time it opened.
Only `Allow` moves Open to HalfOpen (when the break is over); only `Success` and `Failure` leave HalfOpen.
template: Dojo.Eq("a success resets the count", "Closed", dojoB.State);
Dojo.Eq("three in a row: open", "Open", dojoB.State);
Dojo.Check("after the break: one probe is allowed", dojoB.Allow(10_500));
Dojo.Eq("and the breaker is half-open", "HalfOpen", dojoB.State);
Dojo.Check("no second call while the probe is out", !dojoB.Allow(10_600));
Dojo.Eq("a failed probe opens it again", "Open", dojoB.State);
Dojo.Check("the new break counts from the failed probe", !dojoB.Allow(20_600));
Dojo.Check("and ends 10 s after it", dojoB.Allow(20_700));
Dojo.Eq("a good probe closes it", "Closed", dojoB.State);

steps.title: Admission control by priority
prompt: Write a class `AdmissionControl` that sheds the least important work first:
- `AdmissionControl(int maxInFlight)`;
- `bool TryStart(int priority)`: priority `0` is critical (checkout), `1` normal, `2` best-effort (prefetch).
Admit when the requests **already in flight** are below a share of `maxInFlight`: 100% for critical, 90%
for normal, 50% for best-effort. Admitted requests count as in flight; refused ones do not.
- `void Done()`: one admitted request finished.
- `int InFlight` and `int Shed` (how many were refused).
With `maxInFlight` 10: best-effort is refused from 5 in flight, normal from 9, critical only at 10.
solution: public int InFlight { get; private set; }
public int Shed { get; private set; }
if (InFlight * 100 < maxInFlight * percent) { InFlight++; return true; }
hints: Map the priority to a percentage with a `switch` expression and compare in whole numbers, `InFlight * 100 < maxInFlight * percent`, so no floating-point rounding sneaks in.
Only admitted requests increase `InFlight`; `Done` decreases it, never below 0.
template: Dojo.Check("the sixth best-effort request is shed", !dojoA.TryStart(2));
Dojo.Eq("normal work fits up to 9", 9, dojoA.InFlight);
Dojo.Check("the tenth normal request is shed", !dojoA.TryStart(1));
Dojo.Check("critical work still gets the last slot", dojoA.TryStart(0));
Dojo.Check("at the limit even critical work is refused", !dojoA.TryStart(0));
dojoA.Done(); dojoA.Done(); dojoA.Done(); dojoA.Done(); dojoA.Done(); dojoA.Done();
Dojo.Check("after requests finish, best-effort is let in again", dojoA.TryStart(2));
Dojo.Eq("Done never goes below zero", 0, dojoE.InFlight);

steps.title: Build it: the retry storm
prompt: In the **System design board**, open *The retry storm*. A one-minute database slowdown plus clients that
retry three times at once leaves the system down long after the database is healthy again. Watch the
dashboard stay red after the slowdown ends, then make the system recover within the goal: a circuit
breaker on the database calls, load shedding at the load balancer, or a retry budget.
steps.explain: The slowdown is only the trigger. Retries and timeouts are what keep the database above 100%. Anything that makes the offered load drop below capacity (shedding, a breaker, a budget) lets it drain and recover; more app servers alone just add callers.
